turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on through, Elise. We'll grab your obs before Dr Shah's ready. Your sister can take that chair.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, thanks. Honestly this feels a bit over the top, I'm alright.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's not alright. I'm Karen, her sister. I booked it 'cause she kept putting it off.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): No worries. Arm out straight, cuff's going on.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): First one's one-forty over ninety... ah, the cuff had twisted on your sleeve. Doing it again. One hundred and twenty-eight over eighty-two.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): See? Normal. Told her I was fine.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): Pulse is ninety-two, oxygen sats ninety-eight percent, temp thirty-six point six, respirations sixteen.
[SEG0008] person_1 (NURSE): Weight on our scales is seventy-four point five kilograms.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Elise, I'm Dr Shah. Karen, glad you came with her. What's been going on, from your side?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Not much, truly. I'm a bit tired. Work's flat out. The car park was a shocker too, we circled for ages, but that's not a medical thing.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was asleep in the car before we'd even found a spot. And look how pale she is.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long's the tiredness been there?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Um. I can't pin a start on it. It just crept up. There's no date.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Karen mentioned getting puffed. Are you short of breath?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I wouldn't call it breathless.
[SEG0016] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She stops halfway up the stairs at the school. Every time.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Even a little — on stairs, or bringing the washing in?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, the stairs at work, yeah. By the top I'm puffing. It's minor. I just go slower.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with that?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Heart racing, or thumping in your chest?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Nope. Nothing like that.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Dizziness, or feeling like you'll faint?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I don't get dizzy.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Your GP's note says the periods are heavy. What have they been like?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit heavier, I suppose. Not a big deal. Everyone has a heavy month.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She leaks at work. There's a stash of pads in the desk drawer, been there for ages.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long have they actually been heavy?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): About six months.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Wait, no, I'm messing that up. Six months is when I told Karen. It's been a year. A full year.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): On a heavy day, how many pads?

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't really count. Four or five-ish pads, maybe, plus a liner, over about a week of bleeding, and there are clots some cycles. Couldn't give you a size. Some days it's less than that.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's downplaying the clots. I've seen them. She just waves it off.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): How many days do you bleed?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): About a week now. Used to be four days, years back. Sometimes it runs a day over.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any bleeding between periods, or after sex?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing in between, and not after sex.
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): Pain with the periods?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Bit crampy on day one. Panadol sorts it. Hardly worth mentioning.
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): The referral also mentioned your hair.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit comes out in the shower. I'm not going bald or anything. I'm forty-one, I reckon it's just getting older.
[SEG0042] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The shower drain disagrees. And Mum had thyroid trouble, the underactive kind. Hair was part of that for her.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): Anyone else in the family with thyroid disease, anaemia, or heavy periods?
[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Just Mum for the thyroid. No one else I know of.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): What medicines do you take?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Just iron, sometimes. Ferrous sulfate. The two hundred milligram tablets, when I remember — a couple of times a week, maybe. Not a proper routine.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry to jump in. Bottle she gave me says ferrous sulfate three hundred and twenty-five milligrams, once a day. Printed right on the label.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Chemist must've swapped them, then. I still think of them as the two hundreds. And I definitely don't swallow one every day.
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right, so the taking is patchy, and the bottle strength and what you remember don't match. I won't guess a dose.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Contraceptive pill, vitamins, any pain relief besides the odd Panadol?
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): No pill. Nothing else I take regular.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any allergies — medicines, food, anything?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or drink?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked. Wine with dinner sometimes, one glass, not every night.
[SEG0056] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She barely drinks, honestly. And she works full time in the school office, on her feet half the day.
[SEG0057] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with the bowels, or with passing urine?
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Bowels are fine and wee is fine.
[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fevers, night sweats, or weight coming off?
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none of that. If anything I've got a bit heavier. Not fussed about it.
[SEG0061] person_4 (DOCTOR): Pop up on the bed, I'll have a quick look.
[SEG0062] person_4 (DOCTOR): Conjunctivae are pale, tongue's a bit pale as well. Heart sounds are normal, pulse regular, chest is clear. Abdomen soft, no mass I can feel. No ankle swelling.

[SEG0063] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll say it back. Heavy periods for a year, clots you can't size, tiredness with no start date, puffing on stairs, some hair thinning, iron only now and then, and the tablet strength is in dispute.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): It sounds worse listed out. Day to day I just get on with it.

[SEG0065] person_4 (DOCTOR): My working impression is iron deficiency anaemia from the bleeding. That's not confirmed until the bloods are back. With your mum's underactive thyroid, I also can't rule out an underactive thyroid. A possibility, not a label I'm sticking on you today.
[SEG0066] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'd like bloods today: a full blood count, a ferritin, and thyroid function. Those are happening, the nurse will take them.
[SEG0067] person_1 (NURSE): Yep, I can do the bloods as soon as you're done in here.
[SEG0068] person_4 (DOCTOR): On the bleeding, we might arrange a pelvic ultrasound if it hasn't settled in a couple of months. Not booking a scan today.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine by me. Scans are a hassle I'd rather dodge.
[SEG0070] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Can she get a proper script? Left to herself the iron just sits in the cupboard.

[SEG0071] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll prescribe ferrous fumarate — no, scratch that, not fumarate. We'll stay with ferrous sulfate, two hundred milligrams, once a day, by mouth. New script, one clear dose going forward.
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): Once a day. I'll have a go. Don't expect perfect.
[SEG0073] person_4 (DOCTOR): If you're soaking a pad every hour, or you get chest pain, or you feel like fainting, go straight to emergency. Don't sit on it till the next visit.
[SEG0074] person_4 (DOCTOR): Take that iron in the evening, and keep it away from tea and coffee so it actually absorbs.
[SEG0075] person_2 (PATIENT): There goes the afternoon cuppa. Yeah, alright, I can shift it.
[SEG0076] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back in a fortnight with the results. That visit is happening either way. Reception will book it as you leave.
[SEG0077] person_2 (PATIENT): And if the bloods come back normal, I'm done, right?
[SEG0078] person_4 (DOCTOR): If they're normal and you're still tired, we still need the chat. The fortnight appointment stands no matter what the numbers do.
[SEG0079] person_1 (NURSE): I'll walk you round for the bloods, then reception's just past the desk.
[SEG0080] person_2 (PATIENT): Yep. Let's get it over with. I'm sure it'll all be nothing.

spec.situation: Tired, breathless woman with heavy periods for a year; counts pads and clots in vague terms; takes iron 'sometimes'; hair loss; relative mentions thyroid in the family. Blood tests, maybe pelvic scan.
features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

omissions.text: Heavy menstrual bleeding duration/details were incompletely recorded: bleeding lasts about a week now, sometimes a day longer, and used to be 4 days years back.
Current ferrous sulfate use was said to be intermittent: patient takes it only when she remembers, about a couple of times a week, not regularly.
Patient denied shortness of breath initially before clarifying only mild puffing on stairs: 'No. I wouldn't call it breathless.'
Patient denied contraceptive pill use and denied taking any other regular medicines or vitamins/pain relief besides occasional Panadol.
Family history was additionally negative for other thyroid disease, anaemia, or heavy periods apart from mother’s thyroid disease.
Patient reported no weight loss and in fact said she may have gained a bit of weight ('If anything I've got a bit heavier').
Doctor stated the follow-up in a fortnight should occur regardless of whether the blood results are normal.

omissions.text: Initial blood pressure reading was 140/90 mmHg but was repeated because the cuff had twisted on the sleeve; repeat BP was 128/82.

Shortness of breath was initially denied, but after clarification the patient admitted getting puffed by the top of the stairs at work and just goes slower; there is a real discrepancy between the patient's initial denial and later acknowledgment, with the sister also reporting she stops halfway up stairs.

Current iron dose is recorded incompletely/wrongly: the patient said she takes ferrous sulfate only intermittently and thought they were 200 mg tablets, but the nurse read the bottle label as ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily; the doctor explicitly said he would not guess the current dose because strength and use did not match.
